newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand to press on with industrial hub expansion.
newsitem.headline: Thailand to press on with industrial hub expansion.

text.p: Thailand mounted a confidence-building exercise during the weekend, announcing it would not let economic setbacks retard industrial expansion.
The Thai government told foreign diplomats it would build at least $4 billion worth of infrastructure in the next few years in a vibrant industrial hub along its eastern seaboard.

Former Prime Minister Chatichai Choonhavan led a contingent of diplomats and journalists on Saturday on a brief tour of the region dotted with more than 1,000 export-oriented factories in and around its 14 industrial estates.

"We like to show our potential amid current weak sentiment. Projects have been disrupted by past government changes. I want to back this government to be in office as long as possible to help continuity of project implementation," Chatichai said.

Chatichai, chairing Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh's advisory committee, led officials in unveiling Thailand's ambitious plans to make its eastern region the biggest industrial hub in South East Asia by the turn of the century.

The state-run Board of Investment said the region, which attracted 58 percent of a total $76 billion in industrial projects promoted by the government during 1991-1996, would be expanded to cover 11 eastern provinces, against three now.

The eastern seaboard programme, launched in the early 1980s when the country started exploiting natural gas in the Gulf of Thailand, has oil refineries, steel and petrochemical complexes, and hundreds of computer, electronic and auto parts plants.
Its factories will also include, by 1999, four car assembly plants each producing 100,000-150,000 vehicles a year.

Officials said the programme's expansion would include more road and rail links, a 160-km high speed train, massive upgrades of the Laem Chabang and Maptaphut deep sea ports, an aircraft maintenance centre, and a regional air cargo gateway at the sprawling former U.S. airbase at Utapao.
Jesper Hostrup, economic counsellor of the Swedish Embassy, praised the Thai government for moving fast to counter current concern about the Thai economy.

"Problems of the Thai financial and property sectors will not go away quickly. But it is nice to get a glimpse of Thai industries moving ahead, despite the current focus on many negative aspects of the economy," he said.

Thai exports languished in a 0.2 percent contraction in 1996 after they expanded by more than 20 percent a year for most of this decade. Gross domestic product growth eased to a 10-year low of 6.7 percent in 1996 against 8.7 percent in 1995.
The troubled Thai property sector, reeling under a four-year slump, has threatened the stability of financial institutions exposed to problem property loans.
Hostrup said the Thai economy was suffering as it adjusted to the higher level of technology needed to compete with other Asian economic tigers.
Sawanit Kongsiri, deputy permanent secretary for foreign affairs, said the government had sought to convince diplomats that Thai industries remained robust.

But German ambassador, Dieter Siemes, advised caution. He said Thailand should note sluggishness in its export markets and competition from Indonesia, Vietnam and China in wooing foreign investment when planning industrial strategy.
"Most countries in this region compete to attract foreign investment by offering incentives, a factor that Thailand should study carefully," he said.
